scenes.briefing: Find YOU next to a nearby line. Name that ice marking.
cues: Find YOU next to a nearby line. Name that ice marking.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

questions.prompt: Which line is beside YOU?
questions.explanation: Yes, the blue line is beside YOU. The centre red line is farther toward the middle of the rink.

questions.prompt: Which two clues match the marking beside YOU?

options.text: It runs straight across the rink
It runs around the centre dot

questions.explanation: The nearby marking is blue and straight. A circle and a net are different rink landmarks.

questions.prompt: What could you do first, next, and last to name this marking?

options.text: Look at the marking beside YOU

questions.explanation: This is one simple observation routine: look, notice, then name. It is a suggested routine, not the only acceptable order for a young player.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to another spot beside the same blue line.
questions.explanation: The example stays close to the same blue line and moves along it. Other spots beside that line also work.

questions.prompt: Which marking is farther toward the middle of the rink than the blue line?
questions.explanation: The centre red line is farther toward the middle than this blue line. This compares rink landmarks in the freeze; it does not describe movement.

questions.prompt: Which two markings are between the two blue lines?
questions.explanation: The centre line and centre circle sit between the blue lines. The goal lines and end-zone circles are beyond them.

scenes.title: Name the faceoff circle
scenes.briefing: Find YOU near one end of the rink. Look at the marking around YOU.
cues: Find YOU near one end of the rink. Look at the red marking around YOU.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

questions.prompt: What is the round marking around YOU?
questions.explanation: Yes, YOU are inside a faceoff circle. The other choices are straight lines.

questions.prompt: Which two clues help name the marking around YOU?

options.text: It has a dot inside it
It is a straight blue line
It is the straight centre line

questions.explanation: This faceoff circle is round and has a dot inside. The straight lines are different markings.

questions.prompt: What could you do first, next, and last to name this marking?

options.text: Look at the marking around YOU
Notice its round shape and the dot inside

questions.explanation: Look, notice, then name is one suggested routine for this freeze. Young players may use another sensible observation order.

questions.prompt: Place YOU at another spot clearly outside the circle where you could still look back at it.
questions.explanation: More than one nearby spot could support this practice. The example is outside the circle and is not a uniquely correct placement.

questions.prompt: Which landmark is a straight line rather than the round marking around YOU?
questions.explanation: The centre red line is straight. The faceoff circle around YOU and another faceoff circle are round markings.

questions.prompt: What do you notice first about the marking around YOU, and what name would you try?
questions.explanation: A useful answer notices the round red marking and suggests faceoff circle. This is a simple orientation prompt; it does not claim a unique verbal response or assess skating.

scenes.title: Receive and move it away from pressure
scenes.objective: Scan for available space before the next action after receiving.
scenes.briefing: Navy attacks the +x net. YOU have passed toward teammate 1. The puck has not arrived yet. F1 is gold and stands on the line from 1 toward that net. The question starts after 1 has controlled the pass.
cues: Navy attacks the +x net. YOU have passed toward teammate 1. The puck has not arrived yet. F1 is gold and stands on the line from 1 toward that net. The question starts after 1 has controlled the pass.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

sources.title: Hockey Canada U9 Fundamental Skill Development
sources.use: Developmental theme only; exact keys and geometry checked separately.

questions.prompt: Once 1 controls the pass, which space should 1 check next?

options.text: The netward lane where F1 is standing
Space beyond F1 that requires going through F1 first
Space away from F1, including a pass back to YOU

questions.explanation: Check the space away from F1 before choosing the next move. A pass back to YOU can be useful if that lane stays open. Going toward the net is not automatically better when a defender occupies that route.

questions.prompt: Which two things can you see before 1 receives the pass?

options.text: The puck is between YOU and 1
F1 is beyond 1 toward the right-hand net
1 already has the puck on their stick

questions.explanation: The puck has not reached 1. F1 is farther toward the right-hand net, beyond the receiver. Those are the current positions, before anyone makes the next move.

questions.prompt: Put this suggested scan-and-choose routine in order after 1 controls the pass.

options.text: Check support and an open route
Choose whether to carry, pass or keep the puck

questions.explanation: This is one suggested routine for a young player: locate pressure, check support and route, then choose. The scene does not make this order a universal rule or promise that one action will work.

questions.prompt: Move 1 closer to YOU and farther from F1.
questions.explanation: The example moves 1 toward YOU while increasing the gap from F1. Other nearby receiving spots can meet both aims; the puck remains loose in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Who could be a teammate for a return pass from 1?
questions.explanation: YOU wear Navy like 1. F1 wears Gold. Recognizing your teammate gives you an option to check, not a promise the pass is open.

questions.prompt: What would you check before choosing between a pass back to YOU and keeping the puck?
questions.explanation: A useful answer names the current pressure, open space and support, while allowing either action if its lane is available. The freeze cannot establish speed, gaze or a guaranteed outcome.

scenes.title: Compare the support options
scenes.objective: Compare defender proximity before choosing a passing option.
scenes.briefing: Teammate 2 is approaching a loose puck. Teammates 1 and 3 are options to look for after 2 gains control. F2 is gold.
cues: Teammate 2 is approaching a loose puck. Teammates 1 and 3 are options to look for after 2 gains control. F2 is gold.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

sources.title: Hockey Canada U9 Fundamental Skill Development
sources.use: Developmental theme only; exact keys and geometry checked separately.

questions.prompt: Once 2 controls the puck, which teammate is farther from F2?
questions.explanation: Teammate 1 is much farther from F2. F2 is close to teammate 3. That is a cue to check the lane to 1; distance alone does not guarantee a safe pass.

questions.prompt: Which two statements match the freeze?

options.text: Teammate 1 is farther from F2 than teammate 3
Teammate 3 is farther from F2 than teammate 1

questions.explanation: F2 is close to 3 and farther from 1. Compare that spacing before deciding which passing lane to check.

questions.prompt: Put this suggested receiving routine in order for teammate 2.

options.text: Scan for teammates and the defender
Compare which support is under less pressure
Choose a next action that fits the space

questions.explanation: Scan, compare, then choose is one suggested routine. It does not guarantee that the farther teammate is always the correct pass.

questions.prompt: Move 3 farther from F2 while staying near 2.
questions.explanation: The example increases the gap from F2 and shortens the distance to 2. Other positions can do that too; recheck the passing lane rather than relying on distance alone.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is nearer the right-hand net on the overhead board?
questions.explanation: 3 is nearer the right-hand net than 1. The full rink is an orientation picture for this exercise, not a full-ice game rule.

questions.prompt: In a small-area orientation exercise, what would you check before choosing the lane to teammate 1?
questions.explanation: A useful answer checks the lane, F2's pressure and the support around 2 before choosing. This is a small-area orientation exercise, not a full-rink offside test or a guarantee that 1 is the pass.
